issues.legal_issue: The statutory inquiry into title conducted as part of determining compensation does not decide whether particular property was exempt from vesting in the State.
material_facts: Compensation proceedings were conducted for the jagirdar after the jagir lands were resumed.
The claimant disputed whether the tanks and wells were on occupied land and therefore excluded from vesting.
The dispute concerned whether the properties vested in the State, rather than competing claims to title in land already resumed.
issues.conclusion: The compensation inquiry under Section 17 did not extend to deciding whether the tanks and wells fell within the vesting provision or its exemption; the High Court erred in holding that the dispute had to be decided through that inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17, read with Sections 3 and 8 and its place in the chapter concerning compensation, permits inquiry into rival claims to jagirdari title or rights in lands already resumed, for the purpose of determining to whom compensation is payable. It does not cover whether particular property vested under Section 4 or was excluded under Section 5.

rule.if: compensation_inquiry_underway and property_vesting_status_disputed and not rival_claims_to_resumed_land_title

predicates.compensation_inquiry_underway: An authority was conducting an inquiry to determine compensation following resumption of jagir lands.
predicates.property_vesting_status_disputed: A claimant disputed whether particular property vested in the State or was excluded from vesting.
predicates.rival_claims_to_resumed_land_title: Competing claimants asserted title or rights in land that had already been resumed.

issues.definition: When a compensation inquiry concerns whether property vested, rather than rival claims to title in resumed land, the inquiry does not determine the property's vesting status.

issues.legal_issue: Property of the specified kind situated on occupied land and belonging to or held by a jagirdar or another person is excluded from vesting, so the State lacks authority to take possession of it under the general vesting provision.
material_facts: The claimant asserted that the tanks and wells were constructed on occupied land belonging to the jagirdar.
The applicable definition of occupied land included land held on specified tenures, land held as khud kasht, and land comprised in a homestead.
The statute excluded tanks, trees, private wells, and buildings in or on occupied land from vesting, notwithstanding the general vesting provision.
issues.conclusion: If the tanks and wells were on occupied land and belonged to or were held by the jagirdar, they did not vest in the State and the State had no authority to take possession of them.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(c) of the Madhya Bharat Abolition of Jagirs Act, read with the definition of occupied land in Section 2(1)(ix), overrides Section 4: qualifying tanks, trees, private wells, and buildings remain with the person to whom they belong or by whom they are held.

predicates.vesting_dispute_under_jagir_abolition: The case concerns whether property vested in the State upon abolition of a jagir.
predicates.protected_property_on_occupied_land: The disputed property is a tank, tree, private well, or building situated in or on occupied land and belongs to or is held by a jagirdar or another person.

issues.definition: In a dispute about vesting upon jagir abolition, qualifying property on occupied land is not property the State may take possession of.

issues.legal_issue: In writ proceedings, the High Court must independently determine a preliminary fact on which an administrative authority's jurisdiction depends.
material_facts: The claimant sought relief under Article 226 after revenue authorities rejected the claim concerning the tanks and wells.
Whether the properties were on occupied land and within the statutory exclusion determined whether the State could take possession of them.
The High Court quashed the revenue authorities' orders on the ground that the matter should be decided under the compensation inquiry procedure, without deciding the disputed jurisdictional fact.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was required to decide independently whether the claim that the tanks and wells belonged to the jagirdar within the meaning of the exemption was substantiated; if it was, the High Court could direct the State to hand over possession. The cases of Rex v. Shoreditch Assessment Committee and White & Collins v. Minister of Health were applied.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, when an administrative authority's jurisdiction depends on a preliminary finding of fact, the High Court may determine independently whether that fact is established and must not allow an inferior tribunal to determine the limits of its own jurisdiction conclusively. The Court applied Rex v. Shoreditch Assessment Committee and White & Collins v. Minister of Health.

predicates.writ_proceeding_challenging_administrati: A claimant brought a writ proceeding challenging an administrative authority's action or decision.
predicates.authority_jurisdiction_depends_on_prelim: The authority's power to act depends on whether a preliminary fact is true.

issues.definition: When a writ challenges administrative action whose authority depends on a preliminary fact, the writ court independently determines that fact and may restore possession if the claimant proves the relevant claim.
